approachQuestion.prompt: You may delete individual characters from a string s without reordering the survivors. Return the minimum deletions needed to leave a palindrome; an empty or one-letter string is a palindrome. Examples: "abca" → 1; "abc" → 2; "racecar" → 0. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 1 ≤ n=s.length ≤ 1500; lowercase letters; input is read-only. Return only a deletion count.

options.text: Let cost(i,j) be minimum deletions inside inclusive interval i..j, with empty and one-letter intervals costing zero. Process i downward and j upward above i. Equal endpoints use cost(i+1,j−1); unequal endpoints use 1+min(cost(i+1,j),cost(i,j−1)). Retain only the row for i+1 and the current row, zeroing the current row before filling it.
options.feedback: Equal endpoints can be preserved around an optimal interior. With unequal endpoints at least one must be removed, and either removal leaves a shorter interval. The iteration order makes both dependencies available.

options.text: Use the same interval recurrence but retain all n rows of interval costs.
options.feedback: This computes the correct result on the whole domain, but retains old states that future transitions never read. Removing those states preserves correctness and reduces auxiliary storage.

options.text: Count letters with odd frequency and return that count minus one, floored at zero.
options.feedback: This allows reordering. For "aabb", all frequencies are even, but the string is not a palindrome; two deletions are required.

options.text: On unequal endpoints always delete the left endpoint.
options.feedback: For "bcba", deleting the right a leaves the palindrome bcb in one step. Always deleting the left endpoint removes b first, leaving cba, which needs two further deletions.

feedback.reason: Use interval endpoints as state and handle empty interiors when shrinking a palindrome.
details: Allocate two n-entry zeroed arrays. For i=n−1 down to zero, clear the current row, leave empty and one-letter cells zero, fill j=i+1..n−1 using the stated interval recurrence, and swap references. Return cost(0,n−1). No substrings are allocated.

Equal interval endpoints can remain together; unequal endpoints require deleting one side and taking the better smaller interval. One-character and empty intervals need zero deletions. Row clearing is real quadratic work in the fixed implementation.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Allocate two n-entry zeroed arrays. For i=n−1 down to zero, clear the current row, leave empty and one-letter cells zero, fill j=i+1..n−1 using the stated interval recurrence, and swap references. Return cost(0,n−1). No substrings are allocated. Analyze this fixed implementation. N=n. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.
Include initialization; treat the stated dimensions as variable parameters within their bounds. Use a word per stored counter or flag, not a packed bitset.

feedback.reason: Triangular interval transitions plus whole-row clears take quadratic time with two rows.
details: The triangular set of interval transitions and n whole-row clears both take quadratic work. Two n-entry rows remain live. Character comparisons and cost operations are constant time; there is no reconstruction, input copying, hashing, or recursion.
“O(N) time, O(N) auxiliary space”: There are quadratically many interval pairs, and n full-row clears also cost quadratic work.
“O(N²) time, O(N²) auxiliary space”: The method retains two interval rows rather than every interval result.
“O(N³) time, O(N) auxiliary space”: Each interval transition uses two or three saved cells directly; no substring is rescanned for each interval.
